title: How personality traits and cultural value orientation moderate the pathway from musical emotional expression to group cohesion in choral rehearsal.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Choral singing is widely valued for building cohesion in community, educational, and well-being settings, yet the route by which emotional expression during rehearsal becomes group cohesion remains poorly specified, and most work still centers on individual feeling rather than on group-level interaction. Grounded in emotional contagion and social identity theory, this study proposes and tests a dual-moderated mediation model.
METHODS: We surveyed 612 singers nested within 38 amateur choirs at three separated points in time and coded behavioral synchrony from audio- and video-recorded rehearsals, sampling choirs in two Chinese regions chosen to maximize variation in individualism-collectivism rather than to represent two national cultures.
RESULTS: Multilevel structural equation modeling supported a serial pathway: musical emotional expression raised group cohesion through behavioral synchrony and then shared affect, with Monte Carlo confidence intervals confirming the chain and with reversed-order and parallel-mediator models fitting less well. Extraversion and agreeableness steepened the front segment from expression to synchrony, whereas cultural value orientation, measured in each singer rather than assigned by sampling site, conditioned the rear segment from shared affect to cohesion, the conversion being stronger under a collectivistic orientation. Because 38 ensembles buy limited precision at the choir level, a Monte Carlo power analysis accompanies the estimates and marks which of them rest on firmer ground.
DISCUSSION: By giving the expression-cohesion transition an observable behavioral stage, and by locating personality and cultural moderators on distinct path segments, the study joins contagion and identity accounts. Because the design separates measurements in time but manipulates nothing, the implications for choral education and group facilitation are offered as testable guidance rather than as settled practice.
